sentences.text: Gracias. Thank you, Vice-President.
We make this statement on behalf of the Group of Friends in Defense of the UN Charter.
The group reaffirms its unbreakable commitment to the safeguard and the full observance of the principles and purposes enshrined in the UN Charter.

These are the foundation of a democratic, equitable international order based on, among other things, sovereign equality among states, non-intervention in internal matters, and the right for all people to self-determination, sovereignty, and permanent sovereignty over their wealth, natural resources, and the maintenance of peace.
We believe that the building of a more fair and equitable international order requires that we strengthen genuine multilateralism.
This must be based on respect for international law, dialogue, cooperation, and the participation of all states on equal footing.

In this context, we would like to express our firm opposition to all unilateral practice that is incompatible with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, particularly when they undermine the sovereign equality of states, become a hindrance to the rights of their, to development and affect the enjoyment of human rights of their people.

We affirm also that promotion and protection of human rights should also contribute to the building of this international order based on the principles of universality, impartiality, objectivity, non-selectivity, and through dialogue and cooperation.
This must avoid politicization or instrumentalization as a means of pressure against sovereign states.
Thank you very much.

sentences.text: Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the African Group.

The African Group takes note of the report of the independent expert and shares the assessment that evolving international landscape presents both opportunities and challenges for multilateral cooperation and the realization of human rights and development.

For Africa, a more multipolar and polycentric international order should be anchored in the Charter of the United Nations, sovereign equality, non-interference, peaceful settlement of disputes, and respect for international law.
Multipolarity should not lead to further fragmentation.
or competing spheres of influence, but should strengthen inclusive, representative, and effective multilateralism.

We underscore the importance of addressing structural inequalities in global governance, including through meaningful reform of the international financial architecture and greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making.

The African Group further recognizes the value of South-South and triangular cooperation in advancing development, technology transfer, capacity building, and national ownership consistent with national priorities.

We encourage the promotion of what the report describes as embedded multipolarity through inclusive cooperation and mutually beneficial partnerships, while ensuring that any new mechanism remains voluntary, transparent, and supportive of national ownership.

In closing, the African group remains committed to constructive multilateral engagement to advancing international order that is more equitable, representative, peaceful, and responsive to the priorities and aspirations of developing countries.
I thank you.

sentences.text: Vice President, we thank the expert for the valuable report.

As indicated in the report, Cuba suffers for more than six decades from an economic blockade, the most long-lasting and exhaustive in modern history.
The expert also alerts to the fact that this blockade has been increased to unprecedented levels in recent months.
This includes a brutal energy blockade.
The humanitarian consequences are tangible and serious.
We appreciate the valuable recommendations from the expert when it comes to strengthening multilateralism.
Multilateral diplomacy does not merely continue to be viable, but really also essential.
Multipolarity, when firmly based in the principles and right, is an opportunity to bring about a more inclusive global governance that is more inclusive and more balanced.
Cuba supports the proposal from the expert to initiate consultations to create global index for normative compliance.
This would be a practical and voluntary instrument.
This would allow for multipolarity to be incorporated into the UN system.

sentences.text: Mr. President, Angola aligns itself to the statement of the African Group.
Angola thanks the independent expert for his report and welcomes his contribution to the debate on building a more democratic and equitable international order.
We share the concern that the growing divide between the global North and South, particularly in the economic sphere, continues to undermine equality among nations.

Widening inequalities within and among states also expose structural imbalances and international financial architecture and constraints and constrain the capacity of developing countries to fully realize economic and social rights.
Angola, therefore, supports a renewed approach to the global economy that places human dignity and the realization of human rights at its center.

Such an approach should move beyond conditionalities that may restrict national policy space, and should promote fair access to financing, sustainable debt solution, and greater participation of developing country in global economic decision making.

Angola has consistently advocated respect for international law, multilateralism, and international solidarity, while calling for the correction of structural inequalities that continues to hinder equitable development.
At a time of growing geopolitical fragmentation, restoring trust in multilateralism is essential.
This requires strong international cooperation, solidarity, and renewed investment in preventive diplomacy, mediation, and reconciliation.
Mr. Independent, how can the international financial architecture be reformed to ensure greater policy space for developing countries while advancing a human rights economy?
I thank you.

sentences.text: Mr. Vice President, distinguished delegates, colleagues, it's a pleasure to be with you today on the occasion of my first interactive dialogue in the Human Rights Council as Special Rapporteur.
This mandate, at its core, about the rights of ordinary people.

including those who hold no political power and bear no responsibility for the conduct of their governments, who should not be made to bear the human cost of disputes between states, and about the guarantees owed to every person whom such measures reach.
As unilateral coercive measures have proliferated over the past six decades, their cost has fallen disproportionately on people whom the measures were not intended to harm.
Entire populations far removed from the political disputes that gave rise to the measures, and particularly persons in the most vulnerable circumstances.
Over more than a decade, the previous mandate holders have built a substantial foundation for the protection of human rights impacted by these measures.
However, the challenges identified have not diminished.
These include the expansion and extraterritorial reach of the measures, the barriers in humanitarian action due to overcompliance, and the absence of an effective remedy for those impacted.
This moment is one of pronounced strain on the multilateral order, with consequent effects for the work under the mandate.
The world is increasingly witnessing an environment where sanctions are normalized.

The legal standards that govern this architecture are brought into question, and affected populations are less able to count on the protective architecture that the multilateral system was designed to provide.
Excellencies, distinguished delegates, let us reflect, what does this moment call for?

To respond to this context, and drawing on insights from the diverse range of stakeholders and having taken stock of the mandate, I intend to deepen, systematize and extend the human rights-based approach developed.

This approach will more closely connect to the universality of human rights, the everyday experiences of affected populations, the pathways through which harm is produced, and the obligation of prevention, access to justice, and effective remedy, as well as accountability.

Because rights are enjoyed through the ordinary conditions of daily life, my thematic work will be organized around the systems that secure those conditions, including health and humanitarian action, education, access to information and scientific cooperation, digital infrastructure and technological access, finance, development, debt and sovereign assets, climate resilience, natural resources and disaster response, forced migration, the institution of justice and multilateral cooperation, and recovery after measures are lifted.

The geographical scope will reflect the full range of contexts in which these measures have human rights consequences, also comprising less visible contexts, including regional sanctions, regimes, measures whose adverse effects are borne by third states or non-target populations, and patterns of economic coercion that receive limited scrutiny.
I will further examine contemporary forms of unilateral measures, that rely on private actors, produce extraterritorial effects, and generate significant spillover.
Mr. Vice President, pathways to remedy and restitution must be ensured for affected persons and populations.
I will treat remedy as the test of every other commitment.
We'll give particular weight to due process and to new questions coming to the fore, including around the freezing and confiscation of assets.
and will carry forward the normative work already before the Council.
Humanitarian action must function when it matters most.
Exemptions that exist on paper too often fail in crisis.

I will engage with humanitarian organizations, financial institutions, and licensing authorities to ensure that assistance in emergencies moves at the speed of need and that the standing humanitarian exemption established by the Security Council finds its counterpart in unilateral practice.

Measures that reverse development, depress growth, and push states deeper into debt determine the conditions of collective life for populations that have no voice in their adoption, and they engage the right of peoples to pursue their own economic, social, and cultural development.
I intend to examine these effects, including the accumulation of debt under prolonged measures, as questions of self-determination and not only of economics.

Restrictions on access to advanced technologies, including semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and digital connectivity infrastructure, increasingly determine access to the tools of modern economic and social life, and their human rights implications remain largely unexamined.

Mr. Vice President, in my consultations with a broad range of interlocutors, whose views otherwise diverge on the legality and utility of unilateral measures, overcompliance emerged as a constituent theme.
This consistent theme, I see it as a possibility for an opening.
No sanctioning state presents overcompliance as an objective of its policy.
The problem can therefore be approached cooperatively without prejudice to the broader disagreements that divide states.

I will pursue structured dialogue, in particular with states, financial supervisory authorities, business associations, and humanitarian actors on the causes of the practice of overcompliance and the means to correct it.
Victim participation must be a constitutive feature of this mandate.
rooting it firmly in human rights principles.

Because unilateral measures extend across the full range of rights, I also look forward to working in close cooperation with other special procedure mandate holders on transversal issues that their mandates share, drawing on the knowledge accumulated across the system.
To conclude, the record of the mandate documents the human cost of unilateral coercive measures.
That can be counted in lives lost, in development gains reversed, and in futures narrowed.
The violation of human rights is the reason the mandate exists, and reducing that human cost is the standard that will guide my work.
Mr. Vice President, I now wish to say a few words about the report of my predecessor, Elena Dohan, on her official visit to Cuba.
in November 2025 on her official country visit to Cuba.

In her report, the report finds that six decades of overarching unilateral sanctions and their enforcement, often aggravated by extensive de-risking policies and overcompliance, have had a devastating impact on the Cuban population, particularly on persons living in poverty, women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities and persons with chronic diseases.
Cuba faces severe obstacles in access to fundamental rights as a consequence, particularly in relation to food, health, education, international cooperation and humanitarian aid.
and access to essential public services and infrastructure, including electricity generation, water distribution, housing, and transportation.

The report highlights the use of maximum pressure campaigns, threats to third states, companies, and individuals, and the initial designation and subsequent redesignation of Cuba as a state sponsor of terrorism.
These measures run counter to the principle of sovereign equality of states and the principles of peaceful settlement of international disputes and of cooperation in good faith.
The measures against Cuba are already unfolding into a full-blown humanitarian crisis.
I join my predecessor in calling for lifting or suspending all unilateral coercive measures against Cuba.

Mr. Vice President, I wish to conclude by expressing my profound concern regarding the escalating unilateral sanctions being deployed globally, from Cuba to Iran and beyond, and on officials and judges at the ICC, on my fellow Special Rapporteur, and on human rights defenders and organizations.
We must keep collectively at the center of our focus the human cost of these measures and cooperate to alleviate the adverse impact of unilateral coercive measures on the enjoyment of human rights.
I thank you, Mr. Vice President.

As highlighted in my opening statement, this is a moment of truly pronounced strain on the multilateral order.

sentences.text: Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to address the Human Rights Council for the first time as independent expert on the enjoyment of all human rights by older persons.
I assumed this mandate on the 1st of May conscious of the responsibility entrusted to me and grateful for the important work of my predecessors.
I have since participated in the first substantive session of the Intergovernmental Working Group on the Human Rights of Older Persons, and I look forward to its second session in October.
I also thank the Government of Spain for inviting me to undertake my first country visit in November of this year.
Mr. President, Today, I present the first report to the Council on cognitive impairment and the continuing exercise of human rights by older persons.
At this pivotal moment of global aging, cognitive impairment is a phenomenon that grows increasingly frequent, touching the lives of many older persons and their families.
The longer we live, the more different from one another we become, whether in health or other outcomes.
Yet older age is still too often seen chiefly through vulnerability, dependency and decline.
Once that lens takes hold, it can quietly shape expectations, services and even the way people are spoken to.
My report asks what happens to the exercise of human rights by older persons when cognition changes and that change is met by ageism or assumptions of incapacity.
While cognitive impairment is not confined to older age, it may carry particular human risks in later life.
A diagnosis can begin to speak louder than the person.
Others may assume that a voice counts less, that choices can be taken over, or that participation is no longer needed.
I'm grateful to all those who contributed to this report.
One message emerged clearly.
Cognitive impairment does not diminish personhood, human agency, or entitlement to human rights.
As a neurologist, I have spent much of my professional life with people whose memory, language, or ability to make complex decisions was changing.
One lesson has stayed with me.
What changes in the brain and what remains of the person are not the same question.
A person may lose words and still express trust or refusal.
Someone may need help with a decision and still have values, preferences and a life recognizably their own.

The human rights problem begins when cognitive change is interpreted as loss of personhood, when diagnosis becomes a shortcut to incapacity, when an older person is spoken for rather than listened to, or when relationships and preferences are treated as if they had ceased to matter.
Human rights do not become less universal when their exercise has become more difficult.
That is precisely when their universality matters most and is most profoundly tested.
International human right is a law is clear.
Equal dignity, non-discrimination, recognition before the law, respect for will and preferences, participation and free and informed consent continue to apply.
Where support is needed, it should help the person remain present in decisions about their own life.
Autonomy is too often equated with complex independence, yet none of us lives autonomously in isolation.
Throughout our lives, choices are made within relationships of care, trust and support.
Cognitive impairment does not create this reality.
It makes something fundamental about the human conditions more visible.
In the right form, such support helps a person continue to shape their own life.
This may require more time, familiar people, or adapted ways of communicating.
Agency may be expressed in a gesture, a refusal, a habit, a look, or in a preference known over many years.
Families, professionals, and institutions must learn to hear the forms in which a person can still speak.
Participation is also made of ordinary choices.
where to live, whom to see, how to spend a day, whether to go out, whom to trust.
These are not small matters.
Together, they make up a life.
Mr. President, the enjoyment of human rights cannot depend solely on the goodwill of families, caregivers, or professionals.
Families often provide indispensable support.
that cannot relieve states and public systems of their own responsibilities.
Those responsibilities must be translated into what I describe in the report as rights-realising systems.
The responsibility of states must be visible in law and in everyday practice.
States have positive obligations to create conditions in which older persons living with cognitive impairment can continue to exercise their rights to the greatest extent possible.
Health and long-term care services should be organized around the person rather than the disease.
Their success should be measured not only by clinical outcomes, but also by whether people retain meaningful influence over their own lives and relationships.
In my report, I call on States to examine laws and practices that restrict rights on the basis of age, diagnosis or cognitive functioning.

I also call for stronger support to decision-making and accessible communication, meaningful participation and inclusion, action against ageism and stigma, and effective monitoring and remedies when rights are denied.
Older persons living with cognitive impairment must also have a place in shaping the policies and services that affect their enjoyment of human rights.
Ultimately, the test is practical.
Do laws and policies, institutions and everyday practices allow a person to continue to exercise their rights to the fullest extent possible as circumstances change and years pass?

In short, Our task is to make sure that an older person's need for care and support when living with cognitive impairment never becomes a reason to see less of the person or to violate their enjoyment of human rights.
I look forward to our dialogue and to hearing experiences and good practices of States and other stakeholders.
I thank you very much, Mr. President.

sentences.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President, older persons are the most heterogeneous of all age groups.
While many live autonomously and independently, others require assistance or depend on care.

The report concludes that cognitive impairment does not diminish personhood, human agency or entitlement to human rights, but changes how they are exercised and what is required of states to enable their continued enjoyment.
This rights-based approach is consistent and chimes with the EU's commitments under the CRPD and with relevant EU policies.

For instance, the European pillar of social rights affirms the right to affordable long-term care of good quality, concretised in the European care strategy and the relevant Council recommendation on long-term care.
Moreover, the Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disability 2021-2030 guides efforts towards independent living and community-based support.
The European Commission addresses mental health of older persons through a comprehensive life course approach, complemented by EU action on neurological conditions and disability.

Many EU Member States have adopted legislation to ensure human rights-based approaches for older persons with cognitive impairment and to implement policies that give effect to the person's will and preferences across relevant policy fields.
In closing, a question to the independent expert: how can States better support older persons with cognitive impairment in exercising their autonomy and legal capacity?
Many thanks in advance.

sentences.text: Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver the statement on behalf of the Group of Friends of the Human Rights of Older Persons.
This year, we mark the 10th anniversary of the establishment of our group, which has grown into a diverse cross-regional coalition.
We work closely with United Nations agencies and civil society.
We share the conviction that older persons must fully enjoy all human rights on equal basis with others.
On this anniversary, we reaffirm our strong support for the mandate of the independent expert.
Regular dialogue with the mandate is at the heart of our work group here in Geneva.

Over the past decade, the mandate has made a decisive contribution to advancing the human rights of older persons, deepening the understanding of key issues, and anchoring the rights of older persons more firmly within the United Nations human rights system.
Through country visits, thematic reports, and constructive dialogue, it has provided valuable support to States.
As population ages in all regions, This work is more relevant than ever.
We encourage all states to cooperate fully with the mandate.
Mr. Independent Expert, how can states best support the mandate in ensuring tangible change for older persons?
Thank you.

The family has a critical role to play as the fundamental building block of society because the family plays a central role in providing care and psychosocial support, as well as it increases solidarity among generations and ensure that older persons do not live in isolation.

sentences.text: and the report draws attention to a serious risk, namely that when cognitive capacities are impaired, the person may increasingly be spoken for rather than listened to.
The fundamental dignity of each person is neither acquired nor earned, nor does it need to be justified by capacity.
A person is not defined by his or her consciousness, intellect or abilities.
These qualities may weaken or even disappear, but the person's dignity does not fade with them.
The recognition of such dignity takes place above all within the family and the community, where every person is heard and supported.
Dignity is God-given.
Dependence and frailty do not negate or obscure such dignity.
Rather, they are a manifestation of the human condition.
The measure of our humanity is not given by what we can achieve, but by our ability to let ourselves be loved and, when necessary, even helped.
Consequently, older persons living with cognitive impairment continue to hold and exercise their rights, often through supported and relational forms.
It is precisely for this reason that the response should not be substitution, but dialogue, understanding, and accompaniment.
This will enable them to remain active members of society, able both to receive and to contribute.
Thank you.

sentences.text: Thank you.
Ireland aligns with the EU statement and welcomes the independent expert as he begins his new role.
We thank the independent expert for his report.

Ireland is strongly committed to protecting the human rights of older persons, including those with cognitive impairment, to respecting their autonomy and to supporting their independent decision-making.

sentences.text: Thank you, Mr. President.
We welcome the independent expert on his role, and we thank him for his report.
Cognitive impairment must never be treated as diminishing personhood or autonomy, nor as justification for denying legal capacity.
Yet older persons with cognitive impairment are too often spoken for rather than listened to and excluded from decisions concerning health care, finances, living, and community life.
Older persons remain right holders.
They must be supported to communicate their will and preferences, make their own choices, and participate meaningfully in decisions affecting their lives.

They also include concrete measures to prevent abuse, neglect and exploitation of older persons.

sentences.text: Thank you, Mr. President.
Malta aligns itself with the EU statement.

We thank the independent expert for the report, especially its clear recognition that cognitive impairment neither diminishes personhood nor negates an individual's human rights, agency and inherent dignity.
Coordinated action across multiple sectors is important, including social protection, transport, digital technologies, community services and health and long-term care.
It also requires continued efforts to address ageism and reduce its associated stigma.
Creating age-inclusive and dementia-inclusive communities is fundamental to ensuring that older persons remain visible.
Older persons living with dementia should continue to be recognized as active participants in society and in decisions that affect their lives.
Malta supports moving beyond approaches that automatically connect cognitive impairment with incapacity and instead advocates for models of support that uphold and augment independence and autonomy.
The report also highlights the importance of person-centered and community-based approaches.

sentences.text: Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished co-panelists and distinguished participants.
Over the course of these weeks, this Council will hear about wars, repression and horrific violence.
Our discussion today invites us to look at another kind of violence, and it's the countless quiet wars people endure every day in every part of the world against poverty, hunger and exclusion.
These crises may differ in nature and scale, but beneath them runs a common cause, an insatiable competition for power, whether that is military, economic, political or technological.
Over the past five years, about half of the world's countries have increased their military budgets.
While every country has a duty to defend its people, it also has a duty to meet their essential needs.
Increases in military spending often have direct consequences for education, housing, healthcare and social protection, and direct benefits for the military-industrial complex.
Economic inequalities are soaring.
the G20 Global Inequality Report found that since 2000, the richest 1% has captured 41% of new wealth and the poorest half of humanity, just 1%.
In a world of trillionaires, more than one third of humanity lives perilously close to extreme poverty.
A similar share lives in inadequate housing, and more than half fear losing their jobs.
Our international economic and financial systems are grotesquely out of balance and in need of a major upgrade.
Some 3.4 billion people live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on either health or education.

Rising debt burdens combined with inequitable international tax rules, tax evasion and avoidance, and illicit financial flows leave many developing countries with virtually no fiscal space to provide basic services for their people.
Least developed countries and countries affected by conflict and climate change are hit particularly hard.
These funding gaps put people everywhere at risk.
Underfunded health systems, for example, have made recent cholera and Ebola outbreaks harder to contain.
Despite trillions being spent on advanced weaponry, few could credibly call the world I've just described secure.
We are being sold an outdated, narrow vision of security which is more effective in protecting wealth than people.
Mr. President, policies and choices that perpetuate poverty and inequality and fail to address the climate emergency are a form of oppression.
Economic, social, and cultural rights are not merely about salaries.
They are about freedom, agency, and autonomy, all of which are being steadily taken away from people.
Extreme fortunes bring the ability to influence policy, direct public discourse, restrict competition, shape taxation, and shield controversial business models from public scrutiny.
The same G20 report found that highly unequal countries are seven times more likely to experience democratic decline.
My office's own data shows the growing suppression of civic space around the world, environmental defenders and journalists investigating corruption are often the first in the line of fire.
Less transparency and undue restrictions on participation and peaceful protest are meant to close off ways for people to challenge unjust and corrupt systems.
But those who impose them are building a dam.
Unless they change course, That dam will eventually burst under growing pressure as people's grievances spill over into unrest.
In many countries, people, especially young people, are already losing trust in their governments and taking to the streets.
Mr. President, human rights are about redistribution of power.
That is what makes them radical and threatening to those who would rather keep power to themselves.
My office supports governments around the world in implementing inclusive policies that empower their people through education, opportunities, infrastructure, and more.
An educated voter can participate more fully in public life.
A digitally connected person can access information, services, and jobs.
A woman with a secure income can be less dependent on an abusive partner.
Empowered people make society stronger.
And we have already seen it in many places around the world.
Spain, for example, boasts social enterprises that employ thousands of people with disabilities and generate billions in profit.
The country is now investing in its care and support system to promote autonomy and inclusion.
In cities in Brazil and India, Greater participation has strengthened local governance, made policies more responsive, and reinforced accountability.
We need a fundamental rethink of our economic approaches and systems to turn them towards fairness, equal participation, and human rights at every level.
We need to wake up and stop pretending that economic models are working when they are destroying our environment, heating our climate, and fueling unsustainable consumption.
We are running up an enormous debt to our planet and future generations, so it's really time to start paying it back.
That is the basis of my office's work to promote sustainable economies that tackle inequalities and deliver for everyone.
At a time of dwindling development aid, a human rights economy can help countries mobilize domestic resources through fair taxation, smarter spending, and more effective and transparent institutions.
In Bangladesh, for example, we are supporting the tax reform process, including efforts to shift the tax towards more progressive taxation.
We worked with civil society and media workers in Uzbekistan to strengthen their capacity to monitor and assess budgetary decisions.
We need more cooperation, more political and financial support, more resolve and more creativity to take this work further.
How wealth is distributed should be one of the key measures of economic progress.
There is momentum at the international level which we need to leverage.

I welcome initiatives to reform international financial institutions, to tax multinational corporations and high net worth individuals more effectively, to ensure developing countries have a seat at the table in debt discussions, to advance universal social protection, and to address climate-induced loss and damage.
My office will continue working to ensure that the future UN tax convention has a strong human rights anchor.
By working together, including through the Global Alliance for Human Rights, we can advance the human rights economy, and translate its principles into concrete policies and practices worldwide.
I firmly believe this approach has the potential to deliver greater security and more sustainable prosperity than all the military might in the world combined.
Thank you.

sentences.text: Thank you, President, High Commissioner, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen.

It's an honor for me to speak to you this afternoon as president of the Club de Madrid, the largest global organization bringing together former heads of states and government who were elected democratically, who share their experience and their leadership to promote inclusive, responsible, and people-centered democratic governance.
From this perspective, we also approach economic, social, and cultural rights.
Today, there is greater recognition that social protection, health, education, care, and access to water and sanitation are important.
But there is a growing and increasingly growing gap between recognized rights and those rights which people actually enjoy.
Figures show this clearly in 2024. 2.1 billion people, that is one in every four people on the planet, lacked access to drinking water safely managed.
3.4 billion did not have safe sanitation and 1.7 billion did not have basic sanitation services in their home.
These gaps have deadly consequences.
In 2019, at least 1.5 million people died because of preventable causes linked to unsafe water and deficient sanitation.
And just in 2024, over 560,000 cases of cholera in 60 countries were reported.

Structural inequalities, as well as discrimination, continue to condition the few opportunities that millions of people have extreme concentration of wealth, uh, attests to this reality in 2025, the 10% most wealthy in the world, uh, owned 75% of global, uh, wealth, whereas the… poorest 50% only owned 2% of global wealth.
These gaps are not only economic in nature, they also affect our democracies.
The Global Commission on Democracy and Multilateralism, which was set up by the Club de Madrid, underscores that economic, social and cultural rights are not merely outcomes of good governance.
Rather, they are indispensable conditions for the full exercise of citizenship.
Without economic, social and cultural security, democracy runs the risk of just becoming a mere formal exercise.
We should also address the serious problem of corruption, which negatively impacts enjoyment of economic, social and cultural rights.
For example, in the sector of health, corruption gives rise to greater avoidable mortality, lower immunization coverage, people paying more out of their own pocket, affecting the most vulnerable.
Off-the-book payments, bribes, workplace absenteeism, institutional negligence and fraud contribute to health inequalities and act as health social determinants.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the other covenants and the other international human rights treaties remind us that human rights are indivisible.
civil and political rights, economic, social and cultural rights, the right to development, the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.
All of these together make it possible for effective democracy to take place and human development to take place.
We cannot uphold some rights and neglect others.
If states want to implement these principles, they need to have the real means to do so.
The Club de Madrid has defended fairer, more predictable debt mechanisms, greater concessional and countercyclical financing, safer tax systems and more inclusive international financial governance.
But to have resources is not enough either.
What you need to do is translate these into effective rights and see social protection as an investment and It is the backbone of our democracies' infrastructure.

In that respect, we must absolutely strengthen compliance with commitments under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and encourage states to consider ratification of the optional protocol to the ICESCR, given that many of the factors that condition the enjoyment of those rights transcend national borders and call for collective responses.
All of this strengthens the importance of the multilateral system.
More than ever, we need to bridge gaps between international commitments and the implementation of international commitments.
This is exactly where the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights can, plays, or does play a fundamental role.
As former heads of state and government, we know that to convert commitments in outcomes is one of the main challenges of governmental action.

In the current context, where in which budgets are being cut, it's important that we preserve the capacity of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights to support states and to strengthen national capacities.
You can rely on the Club de Madrid.

We will continue to be an ally in this constant effort to keep economic, social and cultural rights at the heart of the global agenda and to ensure that their enjoyment is fully guaranteed and effectively enjoyed, that these rights are fully guaranteed and effectively enjoyed, which is essential if we want to create societies that are fairer and ensure that our democracies are sounder.
Thank you very much.

sentences.text: Thank you very much.
At UNCTAD, we believe that public debt is an essential tool for development.
And the problem is not debt itself, but indeed the conditions under which it was contracted and is being serviced.

Increasingly, what we see in the developing world in particular is high borrowing costs and debt service obligations that are reducing the fiscal space available for governments to invest in the very areas that underpin economic, social, and cultural rights, particularly health, education, and essential public services.
From a human rights perspective then, debt is not separate from the realization of these rights, as the cost of finance affects what governments are able to deliver to their people.
I'd like to share with you a few of our recent findings.

And one of the key things that underpins this in recent work we've done in the last couple of months is that debt is becoming more and more costly and less accessible as a source of development finance for developing countries.

If one takes the span of two and a half decades between 2010 and 2025, you see that developing countries, excluding China, paid an average interest rate that was almost three times higher than that of the average paid by developed countries.
So this trend over two decades is really showing us a systemic issue, and it reflects how markets and creditors assess the risks associated with developing countries.
In 2025, developing countries paid almost US$1 trillion away in interest.
This is just interest on public debt.
This is not the repayment of debt itself.
We see that 94 developing countries are paying such high rates that if they could access markets at the same rates as developed countries, they would save some 500 billion US dollars a year.
I'll give you an example of what $500 billion a year can pay for.
It can pay for 375,000 schools.
It can pay for 1.6 billion children to be fed every day for a year.
So we are not just talking, when we talk of interest, about financial cost.

We are talking about opportunity cost, the resources that go into servicing interest on debts means that we have children that have to forego education or in fact undergo inadequate nutrition and/or inadequate health services.
We see that between 2022 and 2024, developing countries excluding China transferred more resources to external public creditors than they received in financing.
That simply means that all new debt or new loans, new financing, new investments that come into developing countries are being equal or exceeded by interest costs.
So it seems that this external financing is no longer a reliable source for development.
In the public sector, we can now say that 25 developing countries spend more on interest than education, and 49 spent more on interest than health.
In total, in 2024, 3.7 billion people lived in developing countries where interest spending exceeded public spending on health and/or education.
What we see at the same time, of course, is that other sources of external assistance for developing countries has fallen away.
Official development assistance has fallen from 0.37% of combined gross national income from the Development Account Committee to 0.26% in 2025.
all the time moving away from the UN target of 0.7% of GNI.

First of all, we believe that there is room for strengthened integration of debt and macroeconomic policy with human rights conditions and considerations.
We believe that UNCTAD, working together with the Office of High Commission on Human Rights, could actually help develop more fulfilled and complete policies.
Second, we believe that there is space always for continued technical assistance and national institutional capacity.

UNCTAD's Debt Management and Financial Analysis System, also known as DMFAS, currently allows 65 countries to be enabled to produce sound debt management, debt data transparency, and institutional capacity.
And in addition, we think that there is room to reinforce the UN's convening role to strengthen the voice of borrowers and facilitate peer learning.

At the launch of the Borrowers' Platform in April this year, UNSG Guterres said, "I believe the creation of the Borrowers' Platform is an essential instrument in order for there to be change in power relations, and this change is essential for us to have fairness in the international financial architecture."
If we work together, we can ensure that finance finance development on sustainable and affordable terms is not only possible, but can also support economic, social, and cultural rights.

sentences.text: Thank you so much, Mr. President.
It is a great honor to participate in this discussion today.
As a commissioner of the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia, or SUHAKAM in Malay, I am especially pleased that this panel coincides with the 27th anniversary of SUHAKAM as an NHRI.

For more than two decades, SUHAKAM has worked to promote and protect human rights in Malaysia through monitoring, investigation, human rights education and awareness, law and policy engagement, and cooperation with partners.

So HAKAM has consistently recommended to the Malaysian government to accede to the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, henceforth ICESCR, including through studies on the compatibility with Malaysian laws.
Last month, through the Asia Pacific Forum's high level dialogue, SOHAKAM has identified ICESCR as the most strategic priority for ratification.

We sustain engagement with government institutions across Southeast Asia and crucial stakeholders to translate human rights standards and recommendations into concrete policies, institutional mechanisms, and improvements in the enjoyment of rights.

However, as we have heard, in the context of human rights pushback, in a world where inequalities continue to deepen, despite significant advances in human rights standards and development, allow me to share a few key lessons from the Malaysian experience.
First, progress on economic, social and cultural rights requires sustained engagement, clear evidence-based action, partnerships and institutional long-term commitment.
One example in Malaysia concerns the right to health under Sustainable Development Goal 3, clean water and sanitation in places of detention, as well as addressing deaths in custody.

Through monitoring, published research and sustained engagement with authorities, including with the Royal Malaysian Police and the Ministry of Health in Malaysia, our work contributed to the establishment of custodial health units within police lock-ups.

While great challenges remain, this experience serves as a positive example of how sustained monitoring, evidence-based action, and constructive engagement with duty bearers can help transform a human rights concern into concrete institutional reform that improve the lives and dignity of all the rights holders affected.

Secondly, economic and cultural rights through the National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights, or NAP-BHR, Far from being business as usual, since 2025, Suhakam was among the earliest institutions in Malaysia to advocate for this process, beginning with research on the human rights impact of business activities, including particularly in logging and plantation industries.
The adoption of the NAP-BHR signifies Malaysia's commitment to integrating the UN Guiding Principles and Sustainable Development Goal targets into the national policy and governance framework.

Crucially, the NAP-BHR recognises the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and highlights the need to institutionalise the principle of free, prior and informed consent in practice.
Our experience with the NABHR has taught us that advancing rights is often a long-term process of sustained engagement, institutional continuity, and improved collaborations.
Second lesson, that meaningful participation is essential to reducing inequalities and advancing human rights in a meaningful manner.
This has guided SWACAM's work with indigenous peoples, particularly women, children, persons with disabilities and others facing discrimination and exclusion.
Earlier this year, SWACHAM organised a national forum on the rights of indigenous peoples with the support of OHCHR.

The discussions built upon the national inquiry into the land rights of Indigenous peoples, and reaffirm that customary land rights, the preservation of culture and identity, and participation in decision making are central to the overall well-being of Indigenous communities.
A particular highlight was on cultural identity through the mapping and preservation of Indigenous oral tradition, storytelling, and languages.
to preserve that and through the role of the state assemblies in Malaysia to preserve indigenous rights.

As Suhakam is the chair of the Southeast Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum or CNF, we continue to nurture stronger strategic collaboration among Southeast Asian and HRIs to advance the rights of indigenous peoples, strengthen their communities, initiate monitoring of corruption and promote business practices that center indigenous rights and culture.

Similarly, in our engagement on sexual and reproductive health rights and ending harmful practices, among others, with UNFPA, women and girls are not merely beneficiaries of policy decisions, but are active participants in shaping their rights in their daily lives.
The same principles underpin our efforts to promote human rights cities in Malaysia.
which have received support within the Department of Federal Territories.

OHCHR's guidance and in-person support from the ESCR section have been useful for the promotion and strategic collaboration with Parliament, as well as the Malaysian Bar, followed by government officers under the Minister of the Federal Territories.

We are excited to move forward with the state, with the support of HCHR, towards advancing human rights in the local government level and ultimately supporting the federal territories in becoming human rights cities.
However, at the same time, significant challenges remain.
Structural inequalities continue to affect access to healthcare, education, housing, land, social protection, and decent work.
Indigenous peoples, women and girls, migrants, refugees and persons living in vulnerable situations continue to experience disproportionate barriers in their enjoyment of their rights.
We are also witnessing increasing pressure on public resources and institutions tasked with protecting rights.
In many countries, including across the Asia-Pacific region, human rights institutions navigating challenging circumstances, especially economically, as well as resource constraints.
In this context, it is important to mention the unique value of collaboration between SWACAM and OHCHR.
The relationship and engagement have been long-standing, particularly with the Regional Office for Southeast Asia and recently the ESR Knowledge Hub.

So, Hakam will develop a context-specific ESCR monitoring tool with the technical support and collaboration of OHCHR to assess the government commitments towards fulfilling our human rights obligations.
Let me end with a concrete recommendation.
Greater investment is needed in national human rights institutions so that we fully comply with the Paris Principles.

and HRIs are critical partners in monitoring implementation, generating evidence, supporting dialogue with authorities and the United Nations in order that the experience of rights holders truly inform public policy and contribute to regaining rights.
At a time of widening inequalities, strengthening OHCHR's capacity to provide technical assistance and capacity development on ESCR is essential to supporting implementation on the ground.
So, Hakam remains committed to explore collaborative opportunities towards substantive equality and amplifying the Paris principles to advance human rights for all.
Thank you so much.

sentences.text: Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of Australia, Canada, and my own country, New Zealand.
All human rights, including economic, social, and cultural rights, are fundamental to building resilient and prosperous societies.
They are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated, and apply to all without discrimination.
One set of rights cannot be fully enjoyed without the other.
The universal enjoyment of economic, social, and cultural rights faces persistent challenges, as we have heard from the panel.
These include conflict and humanitarian crises, weak governance, and discrimination against marginalized groups.
States bear the primary responsibility for fulfilling all human rights.

Effective implementation of economic, social, and cultural rights requires practical solutions and measurable outcomes, the full, equal, and meaningful participation of all sectors of society, as well as evidence-based decision-making.
Good governance and effective institutions are also vital.
UN human rights mechanisms are key to supporting states to fulfill these rights through technical assistance and capacity building and in holding states to account.
We call for predictable and sustainable funding for the human rights pillar and encourage states to support efficiency and rationalization efforts at the HRC.
International cooperation remains critical to strengthening the realization of economic, social, and cultural rights for all.
We welcome continued dialogue to improve outcomes and to strengthen accountability.
Thank you.

sentences.text: Mr. President, Sierra Leone aligns with the African Group's statements and welcomes this timely panel discussion on promoting and protecting economic, social, and cultural rights in addressing inequalities.
The history of international human rights system reminds us that all rights must be viewed as a whole.

The division of the International Covenant framework into civil and political rights, economic, social, and cultural rights, against the background of the Cold War, contributed over time to an artificial perception of hierarchy between rights.
1993 Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action provided an important reaffirmation that all human rights are equal, indivisible, independent, and must be treated fairly and equally.
We affirm that economic, social, and cultural rights and civil and political rights are equally important.
The realization of one category is inseparable from the realization of the other.

sentences.text: Excellencies, dear colleagues, friends, good morning.
I'm Melissa Fleming, UN Under-Secretary-General for Global Communications, and it is my honor to welcome you to this year's Peace Bell ceremony.
We gather in observation of International Peace Day.
It's commemorated every year on the 21st of September.
And this is a date on which, if only for one moment, we ask the world to pause and reflect on what peace truly means.
For our organization, this day carries special meaning.
It speaks to the deepest aspirations of humankind, and that is to live in a world free of violence and strife.
I would like to begin by thanking the young violinist from Tarumi Program and the United Nations Singers for the beautiful and inspiring music that they shared with us.
The theme of this year's observance is "Invest in Peace for Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day."
And this speaks to a simple truth that the benefits of peace must reach every person in every place on Earth.
And that does not happen on its own.
It takes quiet, often unseen work by community leaders, educators, young people, activists, neighbors, and citizens who choose dialogue over division, cooperation over confrontation.
They are the everyday architects of peace.
And their example shows what investing in peace actually means, not a decision made once, but a practice renewed day after day in ordinary moments and in ordinary places.
And that is the work each of us can continue in our communities and beyond.
It is now my pleasure to welcome the United Nations Secretary-General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, as well as His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the 81st session of the General Assembly.
And we are also pleased to be joined by Mr. Yamazaki Kazuyuki, who is the Permanent Representative of Japan, and Mrs. Yamazaki Yuko.
And finally, it is our honor to have with us Mr. Abe Shin, the designer and the gardener of the Japanese garden in which we stand.
as well as Ms. Takase Saiko, the daughter of the donor of the Peace Bell to the United Nations and also the founder of the Association of the Preservation of the UN Peace Bell.
And I am pleased to note that as part of the Expo 2025 Osaka Legacy Project, essential maintenance work was carried out last month on the Peace Bell and on the Japanese Garden.
which has helped to preserve this beautiful and meaningful place for future generations.

Two plaques have also been installed, one here in the Japanese Garden and another in the visitors' lobby, so that the story and enduring message of the Peace Bell can reach the many people who visit the United Nations.
I would like to express our sincere appreciation to the Government of Japan for its generous support for this work.

Thank you once again for being with us this morning, and it is now my pleasure to welcome the Secretary General of the United Nations, Antonio Guterres, who will ring the Peace Bell after his statement.
Mr. Secretary General.

sentences.text: Mr. Mr. President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, each year, the toll of the Peace Bell reminds us of the most important and consequential job we have: building peace.
Peace is never a perceived achievement.
Peace is hard work.
Peace is action.
But in our world today, action for peace is faltering.
Violence and division are tearing apart communities.
Conflicts are widening and deepening.
People are suffering.
And the dialogue and solidarity that solutions require are missing in action.
But where governments are failing to deliver peace, people are showing another way.
Around the world, volunteers, advocates, civil society, leaders, peacekeepers, and peacemakers are doing the heavy lifting of peace, raising their voices, bridging divides, healing communities.
So their actions, large and small, They are bringing to life the theme of this year's International Day of Peace, "Investing in Peace for Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day."

As world leaders prepare to gather at the United Nations in the coming weeks, I urge them to follow the lead of these champions of peace by investing in sustainable development, in people's health, education, nutrition, and social protection.

by building institutions and systems that people can trust, by safeguarding the human rights and dignity that belong to every person, by recommitting to the proven tools of peace, diplomacy, dialogue, negotiation, and peacekeeping, and by ending wars and conflicts now.
Today, I'll call on world leaders to stand with us, take action, invest in solutions, and do the hard work of building lasting, sustainable peace.
This is the last time I will ring the peace bell, but I will always stand with the champions of peace around the world.
Thank you.

sentences.text: Mr. Secretary General, Ambassador Yamazaki Madam Yamazaki, Under Secretary General Fleming, and all those gathered here at this monument of peace, peace be upon all of us.
I'm honored to join you today to commemorate the International Day of Peace.
Allow me to express my sincere thanks to Ambassador Yamazaki and the Permanent Mission of Japan for maintaining this venerable tradition.
We are privileged to be joined by Ms. Takase Siko, daughter of Peace Bell creator Chiyoji Nakagawa, who proposed his idea to the sixth session of the General Assembly in Paris in 1951.
Moved by an extraordinary aspiration for peace, Mr. Nakagawa collected coins from around the world, melted them, and cast the Peace Bell from the stories they told.
This is what he has done, stories of saving, lives and sacrifice, of solidarity in times of chaos, of hope that the seeds for global peace might one day take hold.
This hope for peace was placed in the hands of the United Nations, where we are standing today, and with it a duty to ensure it was not placed in vain.
In ringing the bell today, we are reminded of this legacy.
and the inescapable truth for which this bell tolls.

Peace must be built, and it is our shared responsibility to build it, through acts of courage and compromise, through choices of unity over division, and the countless individual contributions that give life to our collective aims.
It's not easy, as the Secretary-General said, but this is a difficult task that we must do.
Indeed, to invest in peace is to invest in trust, and 81 years on, in the confidence that multilateral actions can still deliver for those it exists to serve.
This year's theme, "Invest in Peace for Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day," reminds us of this calling.
Like the Peace Bell, the UN was formed in a crucible, from the ashes of war.
It ushered in a new dawn, bringing countries of different histories and cultures together to build something greater than any could build alone.
We see this mosaic represented in the General Assembly, and as President of the 81st session of the Assembly, I take our shared mission to heart.
I will work tirelessly to renew trust among Member States and in this institution.
Excellencies, you may know that beneath this bell are handfuls of soil from Nagasaki and Hiroshima, sent to Mr. Nakagawa by hibakusha, survivors of the atomic blasts of 1945.
Their wish for peace so strong, it is the literal ground on which we stand, a poignant reminder that from tragedy, we can leave something behind that asks more from us today.
As the Assembly enters its ninth decade, we honor their memory.
We make a vow to tomorrow's generations to choose peace over peril, dialogue over division.
We recommit to the hard-won principles of the Charter for which those in San Francisco in 1945 stood in awe.
And we uphold the tenets of international law underpinning all we do.
Like those who came before us, let us cultivate our extraordinary aspiration for peace.
Let it guide us towards a future where each generation leaves to the next a world more worthy of peace.
I thank you.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates and colleagues, I'm very pleased to welcome you to this year's second regular session of the UN Women Executive Board.
I look forward to two rewarding days of discussion and consultation as we stay on course and work to fulfill UN Women's triple mandate.
Please note that the second regular session adheres to the code of conduct to prevent harassment, including sexual harassment, at UN system events.
This document is of integral importance to ensure the safety of all personnel and participants during our events, including the Executive Board.
You can access the code of conduct online.

I would like to extend a warm welcome to Executive Director Ms. Shimma Mahauz on behalf of the Bureau and all Member States, and congratulate her on nearing, or approaching, almost five years in office.

including the update on UN Women's engagement with the UN80 Initiative.

sentences.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished members of the Executive Board.
Good morning to you all.
I thank His Excellency Godfrey Kuyaba, Ambassador at the Permanent Mission of Uganda, for presiding over our Executive Board this morning and for his stewardship and steadfast support.

My appreciation also to the Bureau members, Her Excellency Ambassador Suella Janina of Albania, Her Excellency Ambassador Sophie de Smet of Belgium, Her Excellency Ambassador Aida Kazimlieva of Kyrgyzstan, and serving formally for the Latin American and Caribbean Group, Her Excellency Alejandra Hernandez of the Dominican Republic.
Mr. President, allow me to begin on a positive note by celebrating progress made towards gender equality.
Last year brought renewed commitment to the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action.
and gains for women and girls.
Member states adopted or amended 69 laws advancing gender equality.
52 countries established formal care systems, and women peacebuilders participated in every UN-led peace process.
This is only part of the picture.
The other part finds geopolitical tension fiscal pressure, and a UN system under strain, increasingly defining our operating environment.
Conflict, economic insecurity, climate disruption, and the rollback of rights converge in the lives of women and girls, while women's organizations confront surging needs with shrinking resources.
Humanitarian crises exact their highest price from women and girls.
while their voices and leadership remain too often excluded from response and recovery.
The devastating floods in China and Nepal and the Ebola outbreak remind us that crises take many forms but are never gender neutral.
UN Women continues to work with governments, humanitarian partners and women's organizations to ensure responses reflect women's needs, risks and leadership wherever needed.
Afghanistan remains a litmus test of our resolve, and we are failing, unfortunately.
Five years on, women's and girls' ability to learn, work, and participate in public life has narrowed almost to disappearance.
More than ever, we stand with Afghan women and we support their organizations.
In Sudan, women and girls face drone attacks by day and the threat of sexual violence after dark.
Yet women-led organizations supported by UN Women reach places others cannot, providing protection and essential services.
We need to ensure they are supported.
In Haiti, women fleeing gang violence find that violence follows them into displacement.
With UN Women's support, the government has opened the first state-supported safe houses for survivors, while women's organizations continue providing lifesaving services.

In Gaza, we support local women organizations, provide lifesaving protection, cash assistance, and essential services to women and women-headed households, which now constitute one in four households.
We stay.
in Lebanon, in Myanmar, in Ukraine, and across the 103 countries where UN Women works to serve and support women and girls.
This is our mandate.

Excellencies, we began implementing our strategic plan in January of this year, putting the full strength of our triple mandate to work, to translate international norms into laws, policies, and budgets.
To align the UN system around shared priorities and accountability, engaging 75 entities globally and 125 UN country teams to multiply impact.
And to ensure women's organizations shape action on the ground.
We are already seeing this approach deliver results.

In Albania, landmark reforms translated global standards into stronger protections for women from violence in public and political life, supported by UN Women's policy expertise, UN coordination and partnerships.

In Jordan, we are combining upstream policy advice with technical and normative support to accelerate implementation of the country's modernization vision and to deliver measurable gains for women and girls.
This is a model we will increasingly apply in middle-income countries and beyond.

In Papua New Guinea, we are supporting government and civil society to develop the country's first national action plan on women, peace and security, grounded in international commitments and informed by consultations with women in conflict-affected areas.
In Cote d'Ivoire, Our policy expertise and convening power supported a legal reform doubling maternal leave for public servants to six months and increasing paternity leave from three to 30 days.
Our Safe Cities and Safe Public Spaces initiative has reached 75 cities in 36 countries.
When Women Count began, only 26% of the data needed to track SDG 5 were available.
Today, it is 63%.
In Afghanistan, we helped ensure a 20-fold increase from the Women, Peace and Humanitarian Fund which we are proud to host as UN Women.
We helped for nearly 200 women-led organizations, reaching 350,000 women and girls last year.
Through the UN Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women, we celebrate 30 years of investment in more than 620 women's organizations across 140 countries and territories.
These results, Excellencies, reflect a broader truth.
Civil society is indispensable to our mandate and to our impact.
We work with women organizations and feminist movements to shape laws and policies, to expand their leadership and channel resources to communities.
Young women are central to this ambition.
Our strategic plan is clear.
We will back their leadership, strengthen their organizations, and advance their rightful place in decision-making.
This leadership must extend to the forces defining their future.
And technology and artificial intelligence are defining frontier of gender equality where progress can be accelerated or inequalities entrenched.
Women and girls must actively shape it.
My participation in the Geneva High Level Digital Week this past July highlighted the urgency.
Only 24 of the 138 national artificial intelligence strategies refer to gender.
We will connect policy, evidence and partnerships so digital governance delivers for women and girls.
We must also leverage technological reach and technology's reach.
In the second quarter this year, UN Women's digital platforms gained 1.3 million followers, bringing our audience to more than 18 million, one of the largest followings in the United Nations system.
This reach strengthens our advocacy and mobilizes new generations.
Excellencies, together, these results show the power of our triple mandate.
However, progress for women and girls is not UN Women mandates alone.
It is an imperative of the UN Charter and the entire UN system.
And it should concern us all that gender capacity and resources across the UN system are weakening, while gender equality remains too rarely a standalone outcome in cooperation frameworks.
This is why UNHAT is critical.
As an entity born of UN reform, we know what institutional change makes possible.
Reform must strengthen the gender equality architecture, not weaken or dilute it.
UN80 must deliver a better United Nations for women and girls.
We are determined to see it succeed.

Excellencies, since our annual session, UN Women and UNFPA have completed the additional analysis you have requested on a potential merger and alternative options for greater alignment, impact and efficiency.
Informed by civil society perspectives, the analysis sets out the implications, opportunities and risks of each pathway.
As you determine the direction of this process, we remain available to inform your deliberations.
Meanwhile, we are deepening our collaboration with UNFPA and across the UN system.
And we are engaging throughout UN80 to ensure the rights and needs of women and girls shape every aspect of the reform.
Excellencies, flexible resources remain the lifeblood of our mandate, and we recognize your efforts to protect them.
Current projections show UN Women's regular resources declining by less than 1% in 2026, with other resources declining by less than 5%.
I thank our development partners for their continued support amid difficult fiscal choices and urge you to sustain those investments.
Strong governance, transparency and accountability are how we honour your trust.
At this session, we look forward to the joint working group's update on progress following the joint inspection unit report on strengthening executive board governance and oversight.
We stand ready to support the board as it considers the way forward.
The board's oversight sharpens our decisions, reinforces our accountability and helps to sustain the confidence on which our work depends.
The months ahead will demand the same spirit of partnership.
At the 81st session of the General Assembly, UN Women will drive efforts to place gender equality at its core.

UNGA 81 convenes at a time of strain for multilateralism, yet multilateral action remains indispensable to preventing conflict, to advancing human rights, and to addressing challenges no country can resolve alone.
UNGA 81 must put women's equal leadership and rights at the heart of a reinvigorated multilateralism, more representative, accountable and responsive, advanced through feminist foreign policies.
Our forthcoming gender snapshot to be launched at UNGA 81 underscores a fundamental truth.
When women lead, societies do better.
Yet today, six in every seven countries are led by men.
And for the women who want to change that, eight in every 10 women parliamentary candidates face intimidation or violence.
Through the UNGA Platform of Women Leaders, which we host annually with the President of the General Assembly, we will amplify women's leadership.
We look forward to the Women, Peace and Security Open Debate on October 27th under the presidency of Greece.
The Secretary General's report will assess women's declining participation in peace processes and remind us of what collective action can achieve.
At COP31, we will advance climate policies and financing that addresses impact on women and girls and recognize their leadership.
At CSW71, we will work with Member States and civil society to build ambition to accelerate the Sustainable Development Goals and Agenda 2030.
Excellencies, UN Women continues to deliver for women and girls through our teams across the world, who drive impact with courage and determination amid extraordinary complexity.
They are the face of UN Women, and I thank them all with pride.
Mr. President, before closing, allow me to extend special appreciation to our dear Executive Board Secretary, Mr. Jean-Luc Bourges, at his final session after 15 years in this role.
And this is really his final session.
Jean-Luc, we are deeply grateful for your dedication and all you have given to this board and to UN Women.
You will be greatly missed.
Thank you.
Excellencies, I am also pleased to welcome Mr. Ziad Sheikh, who succeeds Jean-Luc.
Many of you know Ziad through Generation Equality and his leadership of our offices in Nepal and in Jordan.
He has deep knowledge of UN Women, and I know this board will be in very good hands.
Welcome, Ziad.
Excellencies, our focus on the strategic plan is unswerving.
Our determination to make reform work for gender equality undimmed, and our commitment to partnerships unwavering.
The world does not wait for us, nor do we wait for simpler times.
You gave us a mandate that has never been more relevant, and every day, together, we make it real.
I want to thank you all very much.
All the best.

sentences.text: Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, good morning.
I do thank you for the opportunity to speak.
And as requested by the Bureau, allow me to briefly outline the alternative options that UN Women and UNFPA have developed in response to the request from you, our Executive Board.
Thanks to Sarah Hendrix and Rachel Dorwicks from UN Women and Neginah Montienne and Sam Horitz from UNFPA who constructively facilitated the organizational wide input on that.
These options have been developed while discussions on a potential merger remain ongoing and without prejudice to the outcome of those discussions.
Together, we proposed four mutually reinforcing areas of deeper collaboration, underpinned by stronger governance coordination.
First, we proposed more integrated country-level delivery.

where both UN Women and UNFPA are present, this would mean closer engagement in common country analysis and cooperation frameworks, greater alignment of our country planning instruments, joint work plans in targeted areas of complementarity, more coordinated resource mobilization and targeted harmonization of business processes.

Where one of the two entities is not resident, we would also explore more systematic ways to ensure that its mandate and expertise remain available, working through the resident coordinator leadership, UN country teams, and regional and global capacities.
Second, we propose a joint strategic framework on ending violence against women and girls and gender-based violence.

This would provide a common framework of action from global commitments through to country level results with aligned priorities, stronger programming, collaboration and coordinated resource mobilization.

Third, deeper collaboration on SDG 5 data analytics, evaluation and foresight, bringing together our complementarity and complementary capacities to strengthen data systems, produce integrated evidence and analytics, and provide governments and UN country teams with stronger decision-ready knowledge.
Fourth, greater operational and services delivery interoperability.
This could include targeted harmonization of processes, common premises, and shared services.
These areas would be supported by enhanced governance coordination, including closer engagement between our Executive Boards and Bureaus.
Distinguished Board members, during the annual session of the Executive Board, Member States requested additional analysis on both a potential merger and alternative options.
This was shared in late August.
In summary, the analysis identifies potential benefits under both pathways, but with different levels of integration, efficiency gains, transition requirements, and risk.

It found, in summary, that a merger could offer greater longer-term integration, transformation, and efficiencies, while the alternatives would provide more targeted and incremental gains with lower transition costs.

Finally, allow me to note that in our ongoing consultations with civil society, they have emphasized protecting mandates, presence, specialized capacity, sustainable financing, and meaningful partnerships with women's rights and youth-led organizations, and continue to have questions around potential merger.
I thank you.
